review: A true hidden gem as far as turn-based JRPG-style RPG Maker games go. Some of the best art of an indie game I've seen, even from games with much greater budgets, with an extremely interesting world. Is this a masterpiece? Unfortunately not. The combat is fun and fairly engaging, but rather simple and not too difficult. The story is grand and the broad strokes are interesting, but the characters are largely a bit one-note, and there were a few instances where I found myself coming across plot beats out of order and getting confused. A bit of tightening up with the world map and the skill system (especially for the final party member, who becomes sort of obsolete with how late they join) would have made this even better. As it stands, though, I would put this as a very fun and charming game with a world and atmosphere I fell in love with. An easy recommend for the price, even with its flaws.

It's an RPG in the loosest sense. 

Positives: 
- Art is great
- Music is good
- Overarching story and concepts good

Negatives: 
* Not challenging at all for experienced gamers.
* Not much content. 
* Pacing is a through line and there is little to no character building.
* Exploration is not rewarding.
* Side quests result in nothing of benefit.
* Story writing is not fleshed out and often confusing and/or missing plot points.
* Characters help with nothing in narration or moving the story along in any meaningful way.

Maybe focusing on the art and a solid story would have been a route to go, because all the RPG elements are just that, elements. 

Overall this is just not a very rewarding RPG and utterly forgetable. Skills feel like a burden and strategies are so basic you can run through this from beginning to end doing nothing but fight what they throw in front of you. After playing you'll feel like you have accomplished nothing but wasted however many hours you've played, which was ~24 hours total play time for me :/ I felt far more annoyed playing this game than any sense of satisfactory outcome or story payoff. After finished playthrough I felt zero emotional connection to any of the characters or any sense of accomplishment, and that pretty much sums it up.

Basically a JRPG, “The Amber Throne” is most distinguishable by its artistic graphics and beautiful music that you will rarely see and hear in games of this type. You start the game as a warrior-princess just woken up from hibernation into a world in turmoil, and you need to muster your skills, gather resources and assemble your companions to ascend to the Amber Throne and deny your rivals to gain access to its power. The plot is quite intriguing, although the story isn’t exactly descriptive and you’ll need to piece it together from various indices, dialogues and journal entries. Gameplay-wise, it’s what you’d expect from a JRPG: party of heroes exploring the world, finding treasures and fighting enemies. Combat system is also typical JRPG, with your characters having their own set of abilities, and about medium difficulty. The game can last couple dozen of hours, sometimes you’ll have to figure out how to continue as the path is not always obvious. The game is sold at a reasonable price that entirely corresponds to its exquisite style and engaging story, so be sure to try it if you like JRPG in general and are looking for something unusual.

This one is definitely a 'Maybe', but I would not recommend for most people. A quick summary: The story is pretty good, the characters are ok, the mechanics are trash. If you really want to play a JRPG and don't mind a lot of jank then this is an decent option. 

Some major pain points:
-New characters start at awkward levels and with just 2 skills. You get basically half a skill point every level, so the characters you get later on are basically useless unless you want to grind for no real reason.
-A lot of skills are completely useless, and it's hard to determine which are bad until you've already invested points in them. This is made awful as you cannot respec so you are stuck with any bad choices, some which are not immediately apparent to savescum through.
-SP(magic) based skills are extremely under powered. There is no way to effectively get your SP stat high enough to be useful. This means you should only spec into skills with ATK based scaling and use ATK boosting gear
-AGI is OP. You get way more turns when you have more AGI. AGI+ATK based characters are inherently stronger. Other characters are only good for buffs and status effects. 
-The only method to effectively heal is by a character that has the passive to double item effectiveness, and use items during combat. Some skills heal % based HP on hit which is 'ok' for sustain.
-Items are horribly balanced, many being useless and some being extremely OP. 
-There are a good amount of bugs. Was able to get past the ones I ran into, one by googling one by reloading.
-Some areas of the game it's unclear or misdirects where you need to go next. Especially annoying since it's hard to find guides.

There's a lot of other jank in the game as well, but overall I moderately enjoyed it, since the setting is cool, the story was interesting and there was some mildly challenging combat. It would be a very good game if there was some re-balancing and QOL changes, like re-speccing and having new characters start with the correct amount of skill points.
I'd say if you're on the fence about buying it, don't bother.

This is an absolutely amazing, gorgeous JRPG that had me hooked from start to finish. The beautiful hand painted backgrounds really breath life into this game. The main character may be a silent protagonist, but you really feel for her and all of her companions. There heavy themes of racism that this game tackles as  well as people abusing power both for personal and public gain.

The combat is also unique for a JRPG. While it is standard turn based battles like final fantasy, the interactions with the enemies based on the various damage types you do is very unique. e.g. If an enemy has a shield, you can do blunt damage to them to have them lower their defense. If you're fighting a plant, you can do fire damage so set it on fire which makes it more vulnerable. Each and every fight is like this, where you pick and choose your damage types to try to find out what the enemies are weak to. BEWARE! If you do not do this, you will die. This is actually a very difficult RPG and you need to take full advantage of enemy weaknesses to succeed in battle.

This has become one of my favorite RPGs! Though the game has many bugs (most of the game breaking ones I found can be fixed by playing the game in compatibility mode for windows XP by right clicking the game file and finding the setting in properties),  I did manage to finish and love this game! The story and world was dark and engaging. There were many unique game mechanics that i felt help balance and keep me interested in the combat. There was also a lot of optional content in this short and linear game.

The amber throne's world has a history full of conflicts and wars. It felt fairly realistic and many of the characters have grim struggles of their own. Overall the different races accross the small world had different cultures and mannerisms. This world was fun to explore and learn about.

The game had several systems i had not seen in other games. Healing items that could only be used from the menu outside of combat often provided exp boosts for so many battle turns. This encouraged me to use inventory items that i may have hoarded and never used otherwise. Some characters even had passive abilites to learn that doubled the effectiveness of healing items. This kept early game healing items from ever becoming completely useless. The crafting system was also offers many different equipment, permanent stat boost items, and great restorative items to craft at new locations with old equipment and items. I very rarely sold things as many things had a function in crafting. My only major complaint here is some of the plants used as potion ingredients were so beautiful and well drawn that they didnt look like things i could pick up and put in my inventory.

Overall this was a great linear game with hidden goodies along the way. The game is very close to 15 hours long so its realistic to finish even if you dont have a lot of time to game. There were a few points where i was lost on where to go next but once you find where to go the plot strings you through the next locations in a very linear fashion. There were many hidden shops, tiny side areas, and even some key items needed to face an optional boss.

Overall the music and soundtrack for this game speak for itself as heavy strong points but the game has a lot of small things i liked and mentioned in this review that i felt made it a fun experience. I definitely recommend giving this game a shot if your not opposed to having to toggle it into compatibility mode.

[h1] In this world, is the destiny of various people controlled by some transcendental entity or wish? Is it like the Amber Throne hovering above? At least it is true, that man has no control, even over his own will. [/h1]

Amber Throne is a neat little jrpg that can take up to 15 hours at least. Yea that's on the storefront, it's true, and at just $15 is a worthy pick up in my opinion, if you can withstand the fact the fullscreen feels super zoomed in and a fixed 640x640 resolution.

That technicality aside, graphics wise it's very pastel to water color styled. It comes to life with the scenery and the sprites in battle. Creating an interesting ambience that betrays the somber, poignant, and almost bleak story. The music helps set this up, which can also be a make or break point, you can turn off the music if it's not to your liking. I say this because recorder isn't for everyone, but the strings are really well done. A lot of the tracks are enjoyable, in my opinion. And the overall quality is a higher cut than what I was expecting for an RPG maker game.

Which speaking of, I point this out because the Amber Throne is basically a powerful wish making device, and as such various civilizations have forged dependence, over-reliance on it. A utopia, eternal life, power and domination, survival and prosperity, everything in between. And they all fell apart when they forgot to enjoy life while they enjoyed its power, yet they continue to seek its power, and care not who they step on to get it.

It's a harder hitting story in that regard. 
A few weaknesses to this game is things don't always make sense in where you're going, you might accidentally backtrack, or wonder around in circles until you get it. This is mostly due to how 'clutter' is arranged, as at one point I wasn't aware a statue hand had just enough pixel space for you to get through, not until I tried everything else to narrow it down.

The other is grammar. Harpsichord sometimes ends up misspelled. There are a few other words here and there where syntax doesn't match up. but it's rare, so it gets a kind of a pass I'd say. The one last issue is there is a rare bug where the ground goes totally black, but this can be fixed by exiting and re-entering the game.

One issue that may make or break is sometimes the battle system is a bit odd, how many effects just turn off upon receiving damage, making some healing effects unusable, meaning a reliance on items, meaning your one guy takes a turn to not attack. And you only get to field 3 people out of a total of 5. It's not unplayable, it just feels wonky, oddly set up. 

So if you're looking for good fights, you're better off looking elsewhere. If you want to experience a story and the world it's set in and the plight of it all, this is for you. All in all not too shabby, especially for the price.

While the production value is undeniable the story seems to be quite underdeveloped, with noticeably amateurish writing.


All of the individual artwork and animations are fairly impressive for an RPG Maker game, the music is a nice touch; the combat actually is quite decent for how simple its framework is. But contrary to how genuine the visuals look, the writing itself is just primitive. The world design feels very much like something a creatively inclined adolescent would write up. It's honestly not bad, but it's not something I would want to dedicate over ten hours or dollars to. The naming of various things is a more obvious sign, such as bland and simple titles like the white-robbed sages. That doesn't sound at all like something grown adults would choose to name a powerful and respected council of government. Meanwhile the story introduces various unexplained lore and unexplained events that leave the player in complete ignorance, it just moves so fast and absolutely nothing is explained. There's no sense of mystery or wonder, it's just confounding in a way that makes the story less enjoyable because it's not understandable. It feels very much like it's trying to be a deeply written world but it's just not crafted well enough to get there.

The primitive world design is amplified by such events as the player infiltrating a city by simply walking to the right of the front gate, climbing up some walls and dropping down. That's just not how reality works, you don't infiltrate a fortified city by just climbing over some rough patches on the wall; especially not directly beside the front gate as well. They try to validate it by saying the guards haven't found this place yet; but it's literally right beside the front gates. There's even a woman sitting on the walls playing a flute over the city, and they say the guards have never noticed this place. It's just not a believable or logical thing to have happen, which is why it doesn't happen in the average story.

The writing itself is simple, when characters speak they all just sound like the developer speaking to the player. They all have the exact same speech patterns, with the exact same relatively simple vocabulary, and anytime they don't it just sounds like the writer is putting on an act to try to make their writing sound a little different. First and foremost, I was drawn to The Amber Throne because of it's art style, and on that front it did not disappoint. It's a beautiful game in both visuals and music, and the main reason I played through the entire game. However, if you want to play this game to enjoy the story, you may be left rather confused as to what's going on. In my opinion, the game is often unclear as to what's going on beyond the world building, and your direction is unclear. I had to rely on the main character's journal to gleam the villain's actions, motives, and where to go next. In addition, the ending left me unsatisfied and a poor fit to the arc of the characters. So if you're looking for a game with an interesting story, The Amber Throne might leave a bad taste in your mouth at the end.

Amber Throne's art is easily the best part of the game. It's all hand-painted and gorgeous, and it alone was what drew me to the game. It sometimes uses default assets for icons and a *single* animation in the end, but for the most part, it is 100% custom.

The story is very interesting and tackles some interesting ideas about how regulations bind us, how we should forge our own destinies, and how you should let go of vengeful desires instead of let them consume you. I don't know if I can really call any part of it "cheesy", it felt really original overall, and I had a great time experiencing it. The worldbuilding is also very nice, and I love how many of the characters are written; I *still* want to punch some of the villains in the face, and I'm going to miss reading some of the words of the party members.

The music was *very* nice, having what felt like it had to be around 40-50 tracks, if not more. Each one fits the circumstances you hear it in quite well, and while I do think that some of the ones you hear a lot (such as the overworld theme) can get too repetitive after a while, it's overall very nice. I wouldn't feel bad about buying the soundtrack.

Combat-wise, the Amber Throne definitely tries to feel different compared to most other RPGs. Five characters with a party size of three (although one PC must be in the party at all times), and each party member has 8 skill slots, with about 24 skills to choose from as you wish on each character, means that your party can really be customized a lot. Many enemies are dynamically impacted by creative use of skills, such as using defense-lowering skills to break the shield of one enemy, or using a gun skill to make a soldier bleed as you shot him in the gut. This aspect is really nice for the most part.
However, I did have *some* gripes with the combat;

- In about the last third of the game, the encounters start to feel more like endurance than actual difficulty; you'll go through corridors with enemies faster than you, that you can't avoid, and fight the same encounter of 2 (or 3 sometimes) enemies several times in the span of 30 minutes. These fights DO give you a good amount of XP, but frankly, the game would be better off without them.

- You're given one of the party members, Sirra, about halfway through the game, and the last one, Oboa, in the last *fourth*. Due to the skill system combined with slow levelling, it means that if you don't grind, Sirra will only have about 3 skills until the last fourth or so, and Oboa will have like *one* for the entire game, maybe two. Admittedly, their base skills are pretty good, but this still does make it almost feel like the game wants you to stick with the first 2 party members, Popelle and Nuo, as they'll have way more skills unlocked just through playing. Despite that, I still was able to use Sirra very effectively once I unlocked him; no idea if Oboa would feel tolerable enough, but from what I've seen of his skill list, he sounds like a lot of fun if you grind for him.

- There's absolutely no healing magic (aside from lifesteal). This is kind of nice, because you never feel that there's an "essential" party member you *must* have, but it also means that if you don't stock up on healing items, you might not be able to beat a boss you're perfectly leveled for (which, frankly, is most of them - this game doesn't require grinding anywhere from what I can tell), simply due to running out of potions, and have to trek back to a shop. At the end of the game, I had something like 90 or so healing items before the final boss, and ended up with about 60 or so at the end - while it sounds like I overstocked, the final boss just... doesn't actually drain you of them that much? Still, 90 felt *reasonable*, and that's kind of annoying with how much gold that requires you to shill out - you *must* be prepared with too many healing items, or you run the risk of running out.
 
And a last gripe; the game doesn't always make it obvious where you should go. Not in a "cool explore"-y way, but more like a "Alright, I've been wandering for 30 minutes with nothing to do, where the hell do I go?" type of way. Later on, the main character's Journal starts to be a bit more clear about where you have to go at the very end, which makes the last third or so a *lot* easier to actually navigate, but about the second and third fifths of the game can feel like the developers didn't have strong ideas on where to have you go.
 
OVERALL; 8.5/10. While no game is perfect, I still had a really enjoyable time with this game, and I can easily recommend it to most fans of RPGs. Just know that if you lack patience, then this probably isn't the game for you; those repetitive combat encounter segments near the end can *really* make minutes feel like hours.

The Amber throne takes place in a mostly drying desert land. The Red kingdom, the kingdom of the humans seek the titular throne. They are not alone in this pursuit, the Sehr empire made up of lizard people is also in the running. The last one in this contest is our playable character Arra the daughter of the last know[spoiler]amber god[/spoiler] , tasked by her father to destroy the throne.

The game’s theme centers on the weakness of the heart, to always seek the most easy and comfortable even to the point that it will hurt ourselves. This is showcased in the use of racism, over obsession of a pursuit or in holding on to stagnant views or ideas. As such the game has a somber or melancholy tone to it.

As for the members of your party, other than talking about the plot points, do not have an active role in game.  In some cases they are interchangeable as they repeat the dialogue.. That was disappointing since you don’t see much of them other than that. The supporting characters are mostly there for the sake of plot progression and  in some cases world building. The minor  characters, other than a few eccentric shop keeps are not much to behold. All of the game’s antagonists in one form or a another embodies the theme of the game than any other character in the game.

Despite the main cast not being at the forefront, the interesting setting and the story and ideas that take place in it make up for that. 

In turns of looks, there is not much to say and that is said in a good way. What you see in the steam screenshots is what you get in the entire game:  hand drawn beauty.The amount of detail especially in the non-in game cutscenes just takes your breath away.

The character animation might have anywhere from one to five frames of animation, which give them a point and click charm. Environmental animation are seen a handful of times, otherwise the game is just a beautiful painted picture. Only down side to the amination is during battle, the party members do have animation for all their actions during battle but, foes will only get stance changes with a few bosses getting non-in game cutscenes for their attacks. It should be noted this reviewer is not a student of animation so take what is said here with a grain of salt.

Due to only having a few rpgmaker games under my belt I can’t say for sure what sound is only to this game and what is shared along with all rpgmaker games. In this reviewer’s time in the game, the sounds did not break the immersion.

When you start up the game, the gorgeous art greets you with a non-in game cutscenes. Along with that is the equally wonderful music. This is the type of music that is heard more often in good standard jrpgs. Along with the visuals, this haunted melody invites you to open and relax your heart for an experience that won’t be forgotten anytime soon. Jasmine Cooper is a gem of a composer; let us hope we will hear more from them in the future.  Goldwood Forest and Goldwood Forest Engaged are  great highlights.

It is fair to say the game’s presentation being one of it’s strongest parts.

The game was made with the keyboard control in mind and since the title screen has a button to show what the controls are for the keyboard, this part of the review shall put more time to talking about controls for the use of a controller, particularly for the 360 controller since this was use in the review. The B button is used for menu and cancelling, the X button is to confirm an action or to pick and talk to someone/interact, for the last button the A button just has to be hold down to run and finally the upper right control stick is to move. There is no way to change the output. It should be advised to put the controller in the the PC before starting up the game. While it is possible to use the keyboard in the middle of the game with a controller in, the other way is not while the game is running.

The world map is small and will get even smaller if a certain side quest is done. However the game will use this to it’s advantage by occasionally changing the map. Other than something that is between the player and the next plot point, the world map holds small places for side quests, world building and some items.

Towns while visually distinct just hold the usual set of items, weapons, armors and inns. Sometimes they have items and other kinds of shops you can find there, but that is about it. While you can talk to the people in the towns and there are some you can give items to, the only place that can be entered are for plot and the above mentioned standard buying stuff.

Dungeons are just a chance to take in more of the art with just more battles. The most that happens was to go one way or the other to fight a mini boss to progress. The last dungeon being the one to be somewhat different. 

Battles, like many things in the game, felt like they are just there to serve the art and the story. It may not be as simple as press A to win, but the player can be left with wanting more. Here is how the battles work. There are six types of attack:  slash, pierce,blunt, blast and the only two elements, fire and lightning.  Some party members have the exclusive ownership of ether fire or lightning. Party members also have an attack type as a default attack.They can get other attack types in the form of skill which can be unlock by leveling up and getting skill points. You damage your foes with their weaknesses in two ways, standard and stance. Standard is well standard weakness the enemy have in general while stance damage will happen when a target is in a certain stance. Upon doing so will result in the opponent changing to a stance that will do more damage to the party, but will leave them in a more vulnerable state. This may not always occur and other types of non-weaknesses attacks may be needed in order to get that stance change.  In battle the turn order can be seen. The most utility this seem to have is trying to figure out when one of the three party members would attack.

Over the course of two playthroughs, it was possible to get by using powerful non-weakness attacks. The above mentioned battle system, gives this game another thing to stand out from other rpgs, just not enough to call it one of the game’s strengths. Other games such as Skybore or Chrono Trigger can give players a better time with their battles.

Some last minute nit picks and things that could not fit anywhere else: keeping your party's equipment up to date was little pace slowing in an otherwise good paced game. This was very apparent near the end game. Crafting while nice to have as a option, could not as used as much as I like due to the scarcity of needed items to use. While there was nothing that made it to the point of exploit or sequence break there were times I could go to parts of places that should not be possible and sometimes Arra can move a bit before a game cutscene can kick in. There were two major bugs that put the game to a standstill. One occured at the [spoiler]end of sunken city. After the boss battle[/spoiler] and the cutscene that follow when I open the menu the screen behind it want black and stayed that way after the menu close. This happen two times in both playthroughs. The second one happen in the middle of a boss battle that takes place before heading to the final dungeon. During that battle the game crashed. The more minor bugs was when I tried to go to the title screen the game just crashed.This did not happen all the time but, it happen often enough that I stop counting after the eighth time.

There are some nooks and crannies that are yet to be uncovered so if you are looking for a heartfelt experience rather than a challenge to overcome with a interesting story that takes place in a thought out world then this game is a good game to get.

Порой в RPG Maker создаются маленькие бриллианты. Это как раз тот случай. Я никак не ожидал такого уровня, но Amber Throne меня приятно удивил.
+Глубокий сюжет, богатый лор внутриигрового мира. 
+Все члены отряда имеют свой характер, свою предысторию, свою философию и место в общей канве повествования.
+Всё в этой игре отрисовано вручную (вроде бы цветными мелками, но я не разбираюсь). Вы не найдёте ни одного стандартного спрайта. Местные пейзажи и сюжетные зарисовки выглядят очень красиво.
+Музыка от Жасмин Купер как всегда на высоте. Обязательно перейдите на сайт исполнительницы и купите этот саундтрек хотя бы за доллар. Такой труд должен быть вознаграждён. 
+Интересная идея с различными стойками для противников и различными типами урона. Скажем, вы сражаетесь против рыцаря. Когда он поднимает щит, он наносит меньше урона, но и получает его тоже меньше, особенно колющего типа. Если в отряде есть персонаж, который наносит дробящий урон, то можно сбить щит, и тогда колющие атаки снова будут востребованы. Противники из дерева будут уязвимы к огню, каменные - к молнии. Такой подход не даёт игроку уныло нажимать в бою на одну кнопку. Всегда придётся думать и планировать. 

С технической стороны же, к сожалению, имеются огрехи:
-Проблемы с балансом. Первую половину игры можно вообще не париться о подборе навыков под различных противников, о грамотных комбинациях, сбиве стоек и баффов. Вы просто будете сметать всё на своём пути. Но вот ближе к финалу сложность увеличится настолько, что придётся нормально так погриндить и заработать на зелья для отряда. 
-Баги. Я не столкнулся с критичными багами, мешающими прохождению, но тут и там попадались мелкие ошибки, как то: непрогрузившиеся спрайты, невозможность крафта определённых предметов на определённом этапе, предметы, которые не добавляются в инвентарь после подбора, ну и так далее. Раздражает, но не более. Благо, что можно сохраняться в любой момент.

It's a JRPG. You probably know what to expect from that, particularly if you troll steam for rpgmaker games periodically like I do. And when you do, you sometimes find a gem like this one.

Gorgeous Art and Sound Design is the first thing that stands out here- Amber Throne is a [i]beautiful[/i] game. Every enviroment I've encountered is distinct and interesting, every enemy and character apart of a consistent and appealing style, and no music track has outstayed its welcome.

To support that, we have a turn-based combat system that's very strong and interesting. Not great about giving you clear instructions to figure out what you need to do, but not overly obtuse, and full of fun ideas. Even the times I've died have felt more like I wanted to take another crack at it than like the game wasn't fair. No Grinding either, which a lot of games like this on steam have been leaning towards lately. Fight the enemies that show up, and you'll be all set, though there is the option to grind if you have to.

Story thus far is a bit vague on a lot of seemingly-important hard details, like who your player character actually is, but does a good job engaging you with what's immediately happening, and making those events work really well. And I've gotten enough of a trickle of information that this seems to be a low burn, not information we're flat-out never going to recieve, which is all well and good. It works well, it's definitely got a direction and themes and interesting places to explore, and I'm very much looking forward to seeing where it leads.

I've also never seen an rpg that made me yell at NPCs to join my party and then have them do precisely not that (at least for awhile) as much as this game does. I'm not sure if that's a compliment or not, but it's certainly a sign of engagement with the characters.

Would happily recommend to anyone who plays JRPGs like this, it's one of the good ones on steam.

[b]The Amber Throne[/b] ist ein klassisches RPG mit taktik orientiertem KS, welches mit dem RPG Maker erstellt wurde

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Das Kerngameplayelement von The Amber Throne ist das Kampfsystem, in dem oben rechts im Bild die Zugreihenfolge angezeigt wird, wobei die Buchstaben die Anfangsbuchstaben der Charaktere in der Hauptgruppe und das Rote X einen Gegner darstellt. Diese wird durch die Agilität der Kampfteilnehmer und deren Aktionen beeinflusst. Techniken, die Aufladezeit benötigen, lassen einen Charakter später zum Zug kommen, als solche, die direkt eingesetzt werden. Meist ist das in der Beschreibung des Skills vermerkt. Am Kampf teilnehmen können bis zu 3 Charaktere, anderen bleiben inaktiv und erhalten weder Erfahrung für besiegte Gegner noch können sie während des Kampfes eingewechselt werden

Gegner haben in The Amber Throne meist mehrere Phasen, die meistens durch bestimmte Techniken beeinflusst werden können und je nach Gegner unterschiedliche Auswirkungen haben. Wenn ein Gegner mit erhobenem Schild zum Beispiel mit einer panzer brechenden Attacke angegriffen wird, senkt er dieses und wird empfänglicher für Schaden. Andere Gegner richten, sobald sie in Brand gesetzt werden zusätzlichen Feuerschaden an.

Das Skillsystem ist ebenfalls ein viel genutztes Element im Spiel. Hier können alle der bis zu 5 Hauptcharaktere spezielle, Charakterspezifische Skills erlernen und ausrüsten, wobei jedem Charakter nur begrenzt viele Slots für Fähigkeiten (Aktive wie Passive) zur Verfügung stehen. Oftmals müssen für einen stärkeren Skill andere, schwächere Skills erlernt werden.

Ein Manko ist die langsame Menüführung. Shops benötigen stets mehrere Sekunden, bevor sich das Interface öffnet. Im Hauptmenü ist es das Selbe. 

Ebenfalls etwas enttäuschend ist der Schwierigkeitsgrad der Kämpfe, da während der Entwicklung offenbar viel Wert auf Taktische Kämpfe gelegt wurde, das taktische Potential der Kämpfe allerdings durch die oftmals eher unterlegenen Gegner und vorallem Bosse unter geht.

Grindlastigkeit ist dem Spiel jedenfalls nicht vorzuwerfen. Gegner erscheinen auf der Karte, es gibt also keine Randomencounter und sofern man stets alle Kämpfe mitnimmt, hat man selten bis nie wirklich Probleme, die Kämpfe zu bestehen. Insgesammt werfen Gegner stets genug Geld ab, um ausreichend Heilutensilien zu kaufen und später sogar Statusupgrades im größeren Stil erwerben zu können.

[h1]Grafik, Soundtrack[/h1]
Die grafische Gestaltung des Spiels ist hervorragend und unter Makergames zählt The Amber Throne in dieser Rubrik wohl zur Spitzenklasse. Ich selbst habe jedenfalls kaum etwas gesehen, was mithalten könnte.
Gegnerphasen sind gut erkennbar dargestellt, es gibt teils sogar animierte Zwischensequenzen und der Artstyle ist konsequent umgesetzt.

Der Soundtrack ist atmospherisch und gut umgesetzt

[h1]Zusammenfassung[/h1]
[b]Pro[/b]
[list]
    [*]Individueller, sehr gut umgesetzter Artstyle mit animierten Zwischensequenzen
    [*]einfaches, aber gutes Skillsystem
    [*]taktische Kämpfe
[/list]

[b]Kontra[/b]
[list]
    [*]Kämpfe bisweilen zu einfach
    [*]langsame Menüführung
    [*]Itembeschreibungen teils nicht korrekt
    [*] kleinere Bugs wie Begehbarkeitsfehler
[/list]

[b]Fazit[/b]
The Amber Throne ist ein Spiel, das auf seine grafische Gestaltung Wert legt und das sieht man auch. Allerdings schwächelt das Spiel im Gameplay etwas, was in Anbetracht des Aufwands, der in den Artstyle gesteckt wurde, doch schon etwas schade ist. Wer sich an leichten Kämpfen und einem langsamen Menü nicht stört und über solide englischkentnisse verfügt, der kann während eines Sales beherzt zugreifen. Die rund 15 Euro sind meines Erachtens etwas  zu hoch angesetzt, darum eine Kafempfehlung von mir nur unter Vorbehalt.

Amber Throne is a turn based RPG in the style of classic rpgs such as Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest, but without the inconveniences that the older titles were plagued with.

The plot revolves around a mute girl who has a single desire, to destroy the titular amber throne, an artifact of great power which can grant the wishes of those who use it. Throughout the game we see the effects of the amber throne on the various races, whether they have had a chance to use it or not. It paints the throne as both good and evil in equal measures, though ultimately, it becomes clearer and clearer as the game progresses that the throne is more than what everyone assumes it is. Along the way you'll meet a colourful cast of characters, each one having varying stakes in the story. Some feel like the Vaan and Penelo of the story, having little reason to go to these insane lengths with a girl who can't even speak. But overall, the entire party fits well. The biggest thing the game has going for it plot wise, is the metaphors it presents throughout the game, I'd list an example, but I don't want to spoil anything. But suffice to say we get to see each nations wish twisted against them in some form or another, and the execution is beautiful for an indie title.

The combat is as traditional as it gets, turn based with menus. Its alot more streamlined than the classics though, instead of having everyone be able to equip all kinds of items and magic, each character has a list of skills they can unlock as they level up. With a set amount of these abilities being equippable to that party member at any given time, forcing you to pick and choose what way you want to specialize that character, but giving you the option to swap abilities out of combat whenever you like. You can have three of the roster of five characters you'll eventually have by the end of the game on the field at any one time, and can't swap them out mid battle. Each combination of characters works in different ways, since you could have all of the debuffers in one group, or the tank, glass cannon and taunting tank in another, and both will work. My personal favourite combo was tank, glass cannon and spellcaster/healer, but that didn't mean I didn't experiment and have fun while doing so. Combat itself is very fast, normally lasting between two or five rounds in random encounters, to about ten maximum for boss battles usually, with the animations for attacks being swift and visually impactful. What little grinding that you might want to do is made painless because of this.

Visually speaking, the game is a mixed bag. Its all hand drawn, but not to an insane, breathtaking quality, at least not all the time. During combat, the art really stands out, both with your characters, and the enemy sprites. The cutscenes shift in quality, but for the most part they look very nice as well, using a slide show format with the text underneath, giving it a slight storybook feel. The overworld map and overworld sprites for everything are pretty simple, but they aren't bad by any means, nor are they good, they do their job and don't look out of place. Though, it is a bit annoying that the quality shifts so much throughout the game, with one part in particular with the final boss really looking like smudges across the screen. 

The music of this game is very simple, no grand scores or epic pieces. To the end the tunes pick up the pace figuratively speaking and get much better, but for the most part the music does its job and it does it fairly well.

Overall I love this game, its everything I could possibly want from a classic inspired RPG, with some added depth. It isn't an RPG in the sense of dialog options or massive impactful choices, but in terms of combat and character developement. The story is what you'd expect from a classic RPG, but with alot more connectivity and substance. You aren't going from one place to another, doing things to get four crystals of the elements, or stop the evil emperor, or save the princess. You have a goal, and everything you do revolves around it, every boss you fight is directly tied to the main plot. Everything, revolves around the Amber Throne. The best comparison I can think of is Chrono Trigger, minus the time travel. While not as perfect as CT, Amber Throne manages to really be a retro rpg, and something much more at the same time. I would recommend it to anyone who is a fan of classic Final Fantasy style games, or titles similar to them.
